section.title: Testing the Spirits
section.sectionRationale: Having spoken of the Spirit God has given, John warns that not every spirit is from God. He gives the test that separates the Spirit of God from the spirit of antichrist: the confession that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh. Believers, indwelt by the greater One, have already overcome the false prophets.
section.thesis: Because many false prophets have gone out, believers must test the spirits by the confession that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh, which marks the Spirit of God against the spirit of antichrist, and they can do so with confidence because the One in them is greater than the one in the world.
section.frameNote: Three beats: the call to test the spirits; the confession of Christ come in the flesh as the test; and the assurance that believers, from God, have overcome those who are from the world.

units.label: Test the spirits
units.note: many false prophets have gone out

verses.text: Beloved, do not believe every {{pneuma|spirit}}, but {{dokimazo|test}} the spirits to see whether they are from God. For many false prophets have gone out into the world.

units.label: The test: Christ come in the flesh
units.note: the Spirit of God against the antichrist

verses.text: By this you will know the Spirit of God: Every spirit that {{homologeo|confesses}} that Jesus Christ has come in the {{sarx|flesh}} is from God,
and every spirit that does not confess Jesus is not from God. This is the spirit of the antichrist, which you have heard is coming and which is already in the world at this time.

units.label: You have overcome them
units.note: greater is He who is in you

verses.text: You, little children, are from God and have {{nikao|overcome}} them, because greater is He who is in you than he who is in the world.
They are of the world. That is why they speak from the world's perspective, and the world listens to them.
We are from God. Whoever knows God listens to us; whoever is not from God does not listen to us. That is how we know the Spirit of truth and the spirit of {{plane|deception}}.

pneuma.gloss: Spirit, breath, wind. Here it refers to the spiritual power or influence behind a teacher or prophet, whether the Holy Spirit or a deceiving spirit. Because unseen powers stand behind human messages, John says not every spirit is to be believed; each must be tested.

dokimazo.gloss: To test, examine, prove, as metal is assayed for genuineness. Believers are to weigh the spirits behind teaching rather than accept every claim. The test is not suspicion for its own sake but discernment aimed at recognising what is truly from God.

homologeo.gloss: To confess, acknowledge, say the same thing openly. The decisive test is the open confession that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh. This is not bare words but genuine acknowledgment of the incarnate Son; the Spirit of God leads people to own this truth, while deceiving spirits deny it.

sarx.gloss: Flesh, the physical human nature. To confess that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh is to affirm the real incarnation, that the Son truly took a human body. It directly counters teaching that the divine Christ only seemed to be human, striking at the heart of the gospel.

nikao.gloss: To conquer, overcome, prevail. John tells the believers they have already overcome the false prophets, not by cleverness but because the One in them is greater. The victory is grounded in God's indwelling presence, giving confidence to discern and resist error.

plane.gloss: Error, deception, wandering. The spirit of deception, or of error, leads people astray from the truth about Christ. It is set against the Spirit of truth; the two are told apart by whether they confess or deny the incarnate Son and whether they heed the apostolic word.

basic.context: John has just spoken of the Spirit God gives, so now he warns: not every spiritual message is from God. Many false prophets are out there. So test the spirits. The test is clear and about Jesus: does the message confess that Jesus Christ truly came in the flesh, as a real human? If so, it is from the Spirit of God. If it denies Him, it is the spirit of antichrist. Believers need not panic, because the God who lives in them is greater than any power in the world, and they have already overcome the deceivers.
basic.hermeneutics: This is the classic passage on discernment. The test is doctrinal at its core: the truth about who Jesus is, God the Son come in real flesh. John is not encouraging endless suspicion but giving a sure measure. The confession is not mere lip service; it is genuine acknowledgment of the incarnate Son, which the false teachers refused. Assurance and discernment go together: believers can test boldly because the greater One indwells them.
basic.originalLanguages: Do not believe every spirit, pneuma, but test, dokimazo, them. The mark of the Spirit of God is that a spirit confesses, homologeo, that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh, sarx. Believers have overcome, nikao, the false prophets because the greater One is in them, and so they can tell the Spirit of truth from the spirit of deception, plane.
basic.typology: The many false prophets going out fulfil the pattern of Israel's false prophets, who spoke their own words while claiming God's authority. The Spirit of truth answers the promised Spirit poured out in the last days, given to lead God's people into truth.
basic.christ: The whole test is Christ: Jesus Christ come in the flesh, truly God and truly man. The incarnation is the dividing line between the Spirit of God and the spirit of antichrist. To confess the real, enfleshed Son is to be from God; to deny Him is to be from the world.
basic.god: God gives His Spirit of truth and indwells His people, so that the greater One in them overpowers the spirit at work in the world. He does not leave His children defenceless against deception but equips them to discern and to overcome, grounding their confidence in His own presence.
basic.crossReferences: Deuteronomy 13 and 18 test prophets by their message and fruit. Matthew 7 warns of false prophets known by their fruit. John 16:13 promises the Spirit of truth, and 1 John 2 and 2 John 7 give the same test of Christ come in the flesh.
basic.oneStory: God has always had to guard His people from false prophets who speak lies in His name. As Messiah's age dawns, the test sharpens to the person of Christ Himself. God gives His Spirit of truth to lead His people, and the confession of Jesus come in the flesh becomes the line between truth and deception in the story's final act.

context.literary:
Verses 1 to 6 are built as a small argument in three moves. Verse 1 gives the command and its reason, verses 2 and 3 supply the criterion, and verses 4 to 6 explain why the criterion can be trusted and who will respond to it. The movement is held together by a steady play on prepositions. Spirits are 'from God' or 'from the world', and the letter leans again and again on that small word ek, 'out of'. The question is always where a message comes from, its source and origin, long before anyone asks how persuasive it sounds.

The passage also answers the end of chapter 3. John closed that chapter by saying that we know God abides in us 'by the Spirit He has given us', 3:24. That phrase raises an obvious problem: if the Spirit is the sign of God's presence, how does one tell the real Spirit from a counterfeit? Chapter 4 begins with that question and ends it in verse 6 with the pairing 'the Spirit of truth and the spirit of deception'. The same two-sided structure runs under the whole letter, light and darkness in 1:5-7, truth and lie in 2:21-22, God and the devil in 3:8-10, and here truth and deception.

Notice the shift of pronouns. 'You' in verse 4 stands over against 'they' in verse 5, and then 'we' in verse 6 steps forward, the apostolic circle that stands behind the letter, 1:1-4. The reader is placed between the false teachers and the apostles and shown which way to face. Verse 6 also closes a loop that opened in 2:18-19: those who 'went out from us' are now described from the other side as people the world listens to.
context.historical:
Travelling teachers were a normal part of the early church. Apostles, prophets and teachers moved from house church to house church, and congregations depended on their hospitality and on their word. That openness was a gift and a danger. Paul had already told the Corinthians to weigh prophecy and to recognise the 'distinguishing between spirits' that the Spirit gives, 1 Corinthians 12:10 and 14:29. A later church manual, the Didache, still spends a section on how to treat visiting prophets, which shows how long the problem lasted.

John writes into a particular crisis. Some members had broken away, 2:19, and were still sending emissaries, 2 John 7 and 10. Church tradition places John in Ephesus in his old age, and Irenaeus, writing in the late second century, describes a teacher named Cerinthus who held that the heavenly Christ descended on the man Jesus at his baptism and left him before the cross. Other early writers, notably Ignatius of Antioch, attack those who claimed Jesus only seemed to suffer. We cannot be sure that John faces exactly these teachings, but his language fits the pattern: the Son of God must be confessed as having truly come in a human body.

In the ancient world a message claiming spiritual origin was rarely doubted on its face. Oracles, dreams and ecstatic speech were common in pagan temples, and Israel's own history knew prophets who spoke by an inspiring spirit, 1 Kings 22:22-23. What made John's counsel pressing was the confidence of the opponents. They did not look like enemies. They had been in the fellowship, and they claimed the Spirit, which is why John gives a plain, public test rather than leaving the matter to inner impression. The letter is usually placed in the last decades of the first century.
context.canonical:
The whole Bible keeps asking how God's people can recognise a true word. Moses gave two tests in Deuteronomy. A prophet whose prediction fails has spoken presumptuously, Deuteronomy 18:20-22, and even one whose sign comes true must be refused if he leads the people to other gods, Deuteronomy 13:1-5. The second test is closer to John's: the standard is loyalty to the God already revealed, not the impressiveness of the messenger. Isaiah says the same, 'To the law and to the testimony!', Isaiah 8:20.

Jesus carries the matter forward. He warns of false prophets in sheep's clothing and says they will be known by their fruit, Matthew 7:15-20, and he foretells that false christs and false prophets will arise, Matthew 24:24. The apostles repeat the alarm. Paul says that even an angel who preaches a different gospel stands under a curse, Galatians 1:8, and tells the Thessalonians to test all things and hold fast to what is good, 1 Thessalonians 5:21. Luke praises the Bereans who examined the Scriptures daily, Acts 17:11.

John's contribution is to put the test in one sentence about the person of Christ. The same criterion appears in 2 John 7 and in 1 John 2:22-23, where denying the Son means losing the Father. The word 'antichrist' belongs to John's letters alone in the New Testament, though the figure it names echoes Paul's 'man of lawlessness', 2 Thessalonians 2:3-4, and the beast of Revelation. Paul supplies the positive mirror image in 1 Corinthians 12:3, where no one can say 'Jesus is Lord' except by the Holy Spirit. Confession of Jesus is what the Spirit produces and what the counterfeit cannot.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
John wants a congregation shaken by departures to stop asking whether the departed were more spiritual than they were. The seceders had spoken with confidence, claimed inspiration, and left behind a sense that the faithful had somehow missed out. John answers with a boundary line the whole church can see. The question to put to any message is what it says about Jesus, not whether it feels powerful or sounds deep.

He also means to restore nerve. A flock told only that deceivers are about will either panic or hide. So the command to test is wrapped in verse 4 with a promise: they have already won, because of who lives in them. The heart of verse 4 is a settled statement of fact, and everything in the passage leans on it.

John also expects the apostolic word to function as a standard. Verse 6 is bold: 'Whoever knows God listens to us.' He does not mean that every church leader is infallible. He means that the message the eyewitnesses delivered, 1:1-3, is the fixed measure against which later claims are weighed. Readers were meant to go away testing newcomers with that apostolic confession, listening for it in sermons and prophecies, and also to go away unafraid when the crowd goes elsewhere. The world's applause is not a reliable sign of truth, as verse 5 says.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
Verse 1 is a command and carries over directly: believers are told to test. The criterion in verses 2 and 3 is likewise given for use. What the passage describes rather than commands is the situation in verses 5 and 6, where the world listens to the false teachers and the faithful listen to the apostles. That is an observation about how truth and error are received, not a rule that popularity proves error and unpopularity proves truth. Many true messages have been ignored by the world and some false ones ignored too.

Care is needed about what the test does and does not do. It is a test of confession about Christ. It does not authorise treating every disagreement as the work of the spirit of antichrist, and John himself never applies it to secondary questions. The marks John names are central: whether the Son has really come in the flesh and whether the speaker stays with the apostolic message. Using the language of antichrist against a brother over a lesser matter would be to misuse the passage.

It also tells us how to apply the command today. The Spirit has not stopped working, but his work is tested by the Word, as the Bereans tested Paul, Acts 17:11. Testing is therefore done in the open, by comparing what is said with the apostolic gospel, and humbly, since the one doing the testing is also someone the Spirit instructs.

debates.question: Who are the 'many false prophets' and what exactly did they deny?

views.label: Teachers like Cerinthus who split the divine Christ from the man Jesus
views.case: Irenaeus reports that Cerinthus taught that Christ came upon Jesus at his baptism and left before he suffered. John's insistence on 'water and blood' in 5:6 and on confessing 'Jesus Christ' come in the flesh fits that scheme, since it denies the union of the Son and the man. This is the traditional reading and it explains why John speaks of Jesus Christ as one person.

views.label: Docetists who held that Christ only seemed to have a body
views.case: Ignatius of Antioch, in the early second century, opposes those who said Christ's sufferings were only apparent. The words 'has come in the flesh' in 4:2 and the same phrase in 2 John 7 can be read as striking at that error. The two readings may overlap, since both deny the true incarnation.

views.label: A general category of deniers, not tied to one named school
views.case: Some scholars argue that John names no system and that we should not push the text into a later heresy. His point holds whichever error was in view: whoever will not confess the real incarnation is not from God. This reading is cautious about what we can know of the opponents.

debates.bearing: The passage does not depend on identifying the opponents exactly. Whatever name the error carried, it denied that the eternal Son took real human flesh, and John treats that as the line between the Spirit of God and the spirit of antichrist.

debates.question: What does it mean that the one in you is 'greater' than the one in the world?

views.label: The indwelling God, Father, Son and Spirit, is stronger than Satan
views.case: The contrast in verse 4 is between God and the ruler of this world, 5:19 and John 12:31. The immediate context speaks of the Spirit of God, 4:2, and of the Spirit God has given, 3:24 and 4:13, so most readers take 'He who is in you' as God present by his Spirit. Verse 4 states a certainty, not a hope.

views.label: It specifically names Christ in the believer
views.case: Some link the phrase with Jesus abiding in his people, John 14:20 and 15:4. This is not far from the first view, since the Father and the Son dwell in believers through the Spirit, John 14:23.

views.label: A promise that believers will not be harmed by deceivers
views.case: Others take it as a guarantee against every deception. John's own warnings, 2:26 and 3:7, show that deception remains a real danger, so the greater power is the ground of confidence and of the duty to test, not a replacement for it.

debates.bearing: God's indwelling presence is the basis of the believer's victory, and the believer's testing is how that victory is worked out. The promise of verse 4 should drive the discipline of verse 1, not excuse us from it.

study.originalLanguages:
The command in verse 1 begins with a negative imperative joined to a present tense: 'stop believing every spirit' or 'do not make a habit of believing'. The verb pisteuo is the same one John uses for saving faith, which makes the sharpness plain. Faith has an object and cannot be given to every spiritual voice. The positive verb is dokimazo, 'to test', which in the wider Greek world described assaying metals. 1 Thessalonians 5:21 uses it for testing all things, and Romans 12:2 for discerning God's will. A test, in this sense, is made in order to approve what is good, not to hunt for faults.

Verse 1 says 'false prophets have gone out'. The perfect tense (exelelythasin) fixes attention on the standing result: they are now out there. The compound word pseudoprophetes simply means 'prophet of lies', and the same word describes the deceivers Jesus warned of, Matthew 7:15. John's contrast between 'going out into the world' here and 'going out from us' in 2:19 is deliberate. The world is where they are headed and where they are at home.

Verse 2 holds a notable grammar point. 'Jesus Christ' is in the accusative and the 'come' is a perfect participle (elelythota), literally 'Jesus Christ having come in flesh'. The perfect expresses an abiding reality: he came and remains the incarnate one. In 2 John 7 the participle is present (erchomenon), 'coming', which most readers take as a timeless description of the person. In both places the point is the same. The incarnation is not an episode that can be set aside, such as a heavenly visit that ended at the cross. Some manuscripts and early writers read 'dissolves Jesus' in verse 3, which expresses the same worry from the other side, since to divide the person is to dissolve him. The BSB follows the shorter reading, 'does not confess Jesus', and notes that the Byzantine and received text expand it.

The word antichristos occurs in the New Testament only in the letters of John, 2:18, 2:22, 4:3 and 2 John 7. The prefix anti can mean 'against' or 'in place of', and the figure in John is both opponent and rival. John says the 'spirit of the antichrist' was 'coming' (present tense, erchetai) and is already present, so it names a spirit, a type, rather than only a single end-time person.

In verse 4 'overcome' is again a perfect (nenikekate): 'you have won and the victory stands'. The word 'greater' (meizon) is also found in 3:20 and 5:9. And in verse 5 the phrase 'speak from the world's perspective' is literally 'speak out of the world', ek tou kosmou lalousin. Their message has the world as its source, which is why the world 'listens' to them, using the verb akouo with a sense of heeding. Verse 6 repeats the verb for those who heed the apostles. Finally, plane in verse 6 is the noun related to planao, 'to lead astray', from which the English word planet comes by way of 'wandering'. The Spirit of truth keeps people on the road, and the spirit of deception sends them wandering.

typology.type: The prophet tested by his word and his loyalty
typology.fulfillment: Israel was told how to treat prophets who might lead them astray, Deuteronomy 13:1-5, and was promised a prophet like Moses, Deuteronomy 18:15. The pattern is a standing test of whether a message turns the people toward the God who brought them out of Egypt. In John the test is sharpened to a confession: the true prophet's word and the true Spirit's witness both honour the Son who has come, Revelation 19:10. Jesus is himself the prophet like Moses, Acts 3:22. The type falls short in that Israel's test was a general standard, while John's is a person, and where Israel's test sometimes produced death for false prophets, the church's test is applied by refusing their message, 2 John 10.

typology.type: The lying spirit sent among Ahab's prophets
typology.fulfillment: In 1 Kings 22:22-23 a spirit is permitted to speak falsehood through four hundred court prophets, while the lone Micaiah speaks the true word. The story pictures what John says in other terms: spirits are real, they may speak in God's name, and the many are not the safe guide. Verse 5, 'the world listens to them', echoes the crowd around Ahab. The escalation in Christ is that the Spirit of truth now indwells every believer, 4:4, John 16:13, and not a lone prophet only. The type falls short because Micaiah's isolation was a mark of Old Testament revelation, while in the new covenant the whole people hold the anointing, 2:20 and 2:27.

typology.type: The great overcoming, Israel at the Jordan and the conquest
typology.fulfillment: God told Joshua that no man would be able to stand against him, Joshua 1:5, and the people entered a land whose peoples were larger and stronger than they. The pattern is a small people, a greater God in their midst, and a victory not their own. John's 'greater is He who is in you' applies that pattern to a battle of truth rather than swords, and Jesus has already said 'I have overcome the world', John 16:33. The type falls short because the conquest was fought with weapons and by one nation, while the believer's victory is by faith, from every nation, and over deception.

study.christ:
The whole passage is held in place by a single question put to every voice: what do you say about Jesus Christ? That is no accident. John begins his letter with what the apostles 'heard, saw and touched', 1:1, the Word of life made visible. The test of verse 2 is the matching confession. The one who came in the flesh was not a phantom. He could be handled. His coming was the beginning of the great reversal, because the Son of God was revealed 'to destroy the works of the devil', 3:8, and so the very point the false prophets would erase is the place where the devil's defeat takes shape.

The confession also protects the work of Christ. If the Son only seemed human, he could not have died as the atoning sacrifice that John names in 2:2 and 4:10. If a heavenly Christ left the man Jesus before the cross, the blood that cleanses in 1:7 was only a man's. The Gospel of John says the Word 'became flesh and made His dwelling among us', John 1:14, and Hebrews says that since the children share flesh and blood, he shared in their humanity so that through death he might destroy the one who holds the power of death, Hebrews 2:14. The incarnation is the necessary precondition of rescue, not an ornament.

Paul gives the same standard from the other side. 'No one can say, "Jesus is Lord," except by the Holy Spirit', 1 Corinthians 12:3. The Spirit has a ministry toward Christ: he glorifies him, John 16:14, and testifies about him, John 15:26. This means that any spirituality that moves the attention away from the real Jesus, however warm it feels, is not the Holy Spirit's work. The Spirit of truth is, in John's phrase, the Spirit who makes much of the Son.

Christ is also the one who has already won. In 4:4 the believer's 'overcome' stands on his own saying, 'take courage; I have overcome the world', John 16:33. The greater One in us is the same who stood on the cross and rose, and who by his Spirit now takes up residence in the people he has redeemed. So the fearless attitude of 4:4 is neither bravado nor a technique. It is the confidence of those who are united to the winner.

A word of caution against over-reading. John does not tell us that the title 'Jesus Christ' as recited aloud is a magic password. The confession in view is a sincere acknowledgment of who he is and what he has done, held with the heart and carried out in a changed life. In 4:15 he says that whoever confesses that Jesus is the Son of God has God abiding in him. Confession and abiding belong together.
study.god:
This passage teaches that God is a speaking God who keeps the truth about himself clear. Because he has revealed himself in the Son, he can be known and therefore falsified, and the church can measure a claim against what he has made known. The God of John is not a vague power. He has a face, a name and a history, and the incarnation is the place where all three meet.

He is also the God who protects his own. The statement 'You, little children, are from God' in verse 4 uses a term of tenderness, the same word John uses elsewhere of the whole flock. God does not simply issue a warning and leave the believers to cope. He puts himself inside them. The Father who gives the Spirit, 3:24, is the one whose presence is greater than all the powers in the world, and the verse shows God's sovereignty not as a doctrine for debate but as a rock under the feet of ordinary believers.

The passage shows God to be truthful. He is the source of the Spirit of truth, and truth in John is not only an idea but a person and a way of life, John 14:6 and 17:17. His truthfulness means that deception cannot finally prevail and that the gospel's claims will bear scrutiny. That is why testing is not an insult to faith. It is faith's partner. The God who is true wants his people to be sure.

It also shows God as the one who exposes the real spiritual conflict. John says that a spirit of antichrist is 'already in the world', and elsewhere that the whole world lies in the evil one, 5:19. God does not pretend that the world is neutral. He names the enemy and sets a limit on its power, which is a form of mercy. The believer who knows the enemy is real, and knows that he has been overcome, is less likely to be frightened and also less likely to be careless.

For worship this passage leads to a steadiness. We do not praise God by crediting every impressive experience to him. We praise him by receiving the Son he has sent, in the real flesh in which he came, and by resting in the One who dwells in us. The test of verse 2 is a doxology in disguise: it demands that God be worshipped as he has actually shown himself.

crossReferences.note: Even a prophet whose sign comes true is refused if he calls the people to other gods, because the LORD is testing whether they love him. John's test is the same kind of test, one that asks whom a message leads to, but now it is pinned to the confession of the Son.

Moses answers the question 'How can we recognize a message that the LORD has not spoken?' with a test of fulfilment. John adds that a message can pass many tests of impression and still fail the confession of Christ.

The prophet sends people 'To the law and to the testimony' and warns that those who do not speak by this word have no dawn. John's apostolic testimony in verse 6 plays the same role for the new covenant: a fixed word that judges every later voice.

Wolves wearing wool, says Jesus, are recognised by what grows on the tree. John's confession and Jesus' fruit go together. The belief a person holds about Christ and the life that grows from it cannot finally be separated.

Paul says no one speaking by the Spirit of God says 'Jesus be cursed', and no one says 'Jesus is Lord' except by the Holy Spirit. It is the positive form of John's test and shows the Spirit's work is always to honour Jesus.

Paul tells the church to test all things and hold fast to what is good. Testing is not hostility to the Spirit but part of how the church honours him, since it follows the instruction in the verse before not to despise prophecies.

The Bereans heard Paul with eagerness and examined the Scriptures daily to see whether his teaching was true. This is a model of the testing John commands: open to the message, and checking it against what God has already said.

Many deceivers have gone out into the world, refusing to confess Jesus Christ in the flesh, and such a person is the deceiver and the antichrist. This is nearly a word-for-word twin of verses 2 and 3 and shows the test was a settled part of John's teaching.

The many antichrists, the last hour and the departure of those who did not belong to us are the background to this passage. Chapter 4 turns the earlier diagnosis into a practical test the whole congregation can use.

Jesus promises that the Spirit of truth will guide the disciples into all truth and will speak what he hears. John's Spirit of truth in verse 6 is that promised Guide, and he speaks consistently with what Jesus and the apostles taught.

Jesus says that in the world his disciples will have tribulation, but they should take courage because he has overcome the world. This is the source of John's perfect tense in verse 4: the victory belongs to the believer because it first belongs to Christ.

study.oneStory:
The question of whose voice to trust is as old as the garden. In Genesis 3 a creature asked 'Did God really say?' and the first humans took the word of a counterfeit over the word of the Creator. Every false prophet in Scripture is a later chapter of that scene. Israel at Sinai, the court of Ahab, the false prophets of Jeremiah's day, and the deceivers of John's letter are all voices that reshape what God has said and win a hearing because they are persuasive, popular or close at hand.

God's answer across the Bible has been to give his people a fixed word and a way to weigh the voices that compete with it. The law and the prophets did this in the old covenant. In the new, the answer is more personal. The Word himself became flesh, 'we have seen His glory', John 1:14, and the apostles who saw him bear witness to what they saw. The test of 1 John 4 is the last stage of a long conversation. It says that the truth about God is no longer a set of predictions to be checked later but a person who has come and can be confessed.

The passage also sits inside the story of conflict between the seed of the woman and the serpent. John says the Son of God was revealed 'to destroy the works of the devil', 3:8, and here the devil's works include lies about that Son. The spirit of deception is the old serpent still speaking. Revelation shows the end of that story: the deceiver is thrown down and no longer allowed to deceive the nations, Revelation 20:2-3 and 20:10. The same book portrays a world seduced by a beast and a false prophet and a people who overcome 'by the blood of the Lamb and by the word of their testimony', Revelation 12:11.

So the verse that says 'greater is He who is in you' is a hinge in the story, spoken in the in-between time. The enemy is real and active, the Spirit is real and present, and the outcome is already settled. In the new creation the testing will end. The Spirit and the bride say 'Come', and nothing false will ever enter the city, Revelation 21:27 and 22:17. Until then the church lives by testing, by confessing and by holding to the One who came in the flesh and will come again.

sermon.title: Testing the Spirits
sermon.why: Begg preaches this passage, 1 John 4:1-6, on the call to test the spirits, the confession of Christ come in the flesh, and the assurance that the greater One indwells believers. A clear, orthodox handling of discernment.

quiz.q: Why does John tell believers not to believe every spirit?

options.text: Because many false prophets have gone out into the world.
options.note: Verse 1: the presence of many false prophets is why the spirits must be tested.

options.text: Because all spiritual experiences are meaningless.
options.note: John does not dismiss the spiritual realm; he calls for discernment within it.

options.text: Because believers can never know the truth.
options.note: John gives a clear test precisely so believers can know the Spirit of truth.

options.text: Because only trained leaders can discern anything.
options.note: John addresses all the little children, not only leaders; discernment is for the whole church.

quiz.q: What is the test John gives for the Spirit of God?

options.text: Whether a spirit confesses that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh.
options.note: Verse 2 makes the confession of the real incarnation the decisive test.

options.text: Whether a teacher is impressive and popular.
options.note: The world listens to false teachers; popularity is no test.

options.text: Whether a message makes people feel good.
options.note: Feelings are no measure; the test is the confession of Christ come in the flesh.

options.text: Whether a teacher performs signs and wonders.
options.note: Signs can deceive; the sure test John gives is the confession of the incarnate Son.

quiz.q: Why can believers face false prophets with confidence?

options.text: Because greater is He who is in them than he who is in the world.
options.note: Verse 4 grounds confidence in the indwelling of the greater One.

options.text: Because they are naturally smarter than deceivers.
options.note: Confidence rests on God in them, not on native intelligence.

options.text: Because false teaching poses no real danger.
options.note: John takes the danger seriously; that is why he gives the test.

options.text: Because they have never encountered error.
options.note: They have overcome the deceivers, not avoided them; the victory is in the greater One within.

quiz.q: Is John's test of the spirits only about correct doctrine?

options.text: The confession of Christ is decisive, and true confession shows itself in heeding the apostolic word and in love.
options.note: Doctrine is primary here, yet inseparable from a life shaped by the truth across the letter.

options.text: It is purely an intellectual checklist with no bearing on life.
options.note: The confession of Christ truly is the decisive test, but John never treats it as bare words divorced from obedience and love.

options.text: It is only about conduct, and doctrine does not matter.
options.note: Here John makes the confession of the incarnate Son the explicit dividing line.

options.text: It has nothing to do with who Jesus is.
options.note: The test is precisely about who Jesus is, God the Son come in the flesh.

questions: John tells us to test the spirits rather than believe every message. What voices or teachers are shaping you right now, and how might you weigh them against the truth about Christ?
The test centres on Jesus Christ come in the flesh. Why is the real humanity of Jesus, alongside His deity, so essential to the gospel you trust?
Greater is He who is in you than he who is in the world. How does the indwelling presence of God steady you when you feel outnumbered or pressured by falsehood?
The world listens to those who speak from its perspective. Where are you tempted to trim the truth about Jesus to gain a hearing, and what would faithfulness look like instead?
Discernment and assurance go together in this passage. How can you grow in testing what you hear without slipping into either gullibility or constant suspicion?

translationNotes.note: 'Confesses that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh' affirms the real incarnation; the perfect tense stresses the abiding reality of the Son having come and remaining in the flesh.
'Does not confess Jesus' follows a shorter reading; the BSB footnote notes some texts read 'does not confess that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh'. The sense of the test is unchanged.
'The Spirit of truth and the spirit of deception' can also read 'the spirit of error'; the contrast is between the Holy Spirit's leading and the influence that makes people wander from Christ.
